summary: This Wikipedia-derived article gives an overview of the European Middle Ages, which it dates from the 5th to the 15th century. It covers the Carolingian Renaissance under Charlemagne, the barbarian migrations and fall of the Western Roman Empire, Byzantine and Islamic developments, the High Middle Ages with its kingdoms, monastic reform and crusades, and the 14th-century Great Famine and Black Death. It also describes medieval education, feudal society, and the Jewish communities' changing fortunes.
one_line: Overview of the European Middle Ages, from the 5th to 15th century, covering the Carolingian Renaissance, barbarian migrations, Byzantine and Islamic expansion, feudalism, crusades, and the Black Death.
key_facts: Charlemagne's court in Aachen was the centre of the cultural revival sometimes called the Carolingian Renaissance.
The English monk Alcuin (d. 804) was invited to Aachen and brought the education available in the monasteries of Northumbria.
Charlemagne's chancery used a new script today known as Carolingian minuscule, allowing a common writing style across much of Europe.
By the reign of Charlemagne, Latin had diverged so far from Classical Latin that it was later called Medieval Latin.
The Ostrogoths received permission from Emperor Valens (r. 364–378) in 376 to settle in the Roman province of Thracia, and Valens was killed fighting them at the Battle of Adrianople on 9 August 378.
In 410 the Visigoths sacked the city of Rome after invading the Western Roman Empire in 400.
The Hunnic king Attila (r. 434–453) led invasions into the Balkans, Gaul and Italy, and the Hunnic confederation fell apart after his death in 453.
The deposition of the last emperor of the west, Romulus Augustus, in 476 has traditionally marked the end of the Western Roman Empire.
The Theodosian Code, the first effort to codify Roman law, was completed in 438, and under Justinian (r. 527–565) the Corpus Juris Civilis was compiled.
By 1100 Roman law was being taught at Bologna, and around 1140 the monk Gratian, a teacher at Bologna, wrote the standard text of canon law, the Decretum.
The Great Famine of 1315–17 was caused partly by the slow transition from the Medieval Warm Period to the Little Ice Age, with excessively rainy years in 1313–14 and 1317–21.
The Black Death, a pandemic beginning in 1347, spread throughout Europe over the following three years and killed probably about 35 million people, about one-third of the population.
Cluny Abbey, founded in the Mâcon region of France in 909, became a centre of the Cluniac Reforms and sought independence by placing itself under the protection of the papacy.
Otto I (r. 936–973) was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 962.
Pope Innocent III (pope 1198–1216) led the Papal Monarchy to its apogee in the early 13th century.
Rome shrank from a population of hundreds of thousands to around 30,000 by the end of the 6th century.
Jewish communities were expelled from England in 1290 and from France in 1306, and from Spain in 1492.

entities.role: Byzantine emperor (r. 527–565) who oversaw the Corpus Juris Civilis, Hagia Sophia and reconquests
